requirements.text: The Framework keeps one version line for a long time. A public name leaves on a calendar, not with a version number: deprecation and removal are dated, and the dates follow a published policy.
A public name leaves in two stages. Compat: it still works, through an alias or a shim, and its replacement is documented. Removed: the code is gone. There is no third, undated state.

Every change that asks a consumer to change anything is recorded in a machine-readable change journal: a rename, a retired value, a removed name, a replaced component, a behaviour change. A change without a record is not released.

A record names each old form and what to write instead, the kind of change, whether the rewrite is mechanical, and, when it is not, an instruction and a before/after example a person or an AI can apply.
A record carries the date it was deprecated and the sweep day it is removed on, computed by the policy: the first sweep day on or after the deprecation date plus the compat period.
The journal is append-only. A record is never deleted; a removed name stays as a tombstone, so a consumer on any older pair can still be upgraded by reading it.
The journal is chronological, so it is also the history of the public surface, readable without the commit log.
Every alias the code keeps (an attribute, a value, an event, a class, a token, a utility, an option) has a record. An alias found in the code without one fails the gate.
On each sweep day every compat record whose date has passed is removed from the code and marked removed. A compat record past its date fails the gate.
A record may be extended once, by at most the policy's extension period, with a reason that names the consumer still depending on the name and the date it migrates.
Compatibility is resolved in shared places (the base's attribute and value aliases, declared alias tables), not scattered through component code, so removing it touches one place.
A page that uses a legacy name gets it noted at runtime, readable as a list (SF.deprecations.list()). The note is silent by default; a page opts in to console warnings.
Upgrading a product reads the journal: a tool finds every old form in the product, rewrites the mechanical ones and lists the rest with their instruction. No upgrade depends on reading prose.
Before a sweep the known consumers are scanned with the upgrade tool and migrated, so a removal breaks nobody who could have been told.
The policy, the journal and how to upgrade with it are published in the documentation for readers, and each record's replacement appears where the component is documented.
The gate holds the journal's form, the policy's dates, the append-only rule and the alias coverage; a browser check holds the runtime note on built bytes.

uses.description: The form of a journal record.
The compat period, the sweep day and the extension rule.
